title: Understanding Diagnostic Failure in Temporomandibular Disorders: A Narrative Synthesis of Evidence and Five‐Domain Framework for Iatrogenic Mismanagement
html:
Schematic flowchart illustrating the Five-Domain Framework for understanding diagnostic failure and iatrogenic overtreatment in temporomandibular disorders (TMDs). Upstream determinants (Educational Deficits, System Fragmentation) create a baseline of diagnostic uncertainty when encountering non-specific TMD presentations. Cognitive heuristics, specifically Structural Reductionism (overreliance on imaging) and Occlusal Overinterpretation (attributing pain to bite anomalies), act as reinforcing biases that convert uncertainty into diagnostic error. Amplified by external drivers (financial incentives, defensive practice, and patient anxiety), this results in an overtreatment cascade of non-indicated, irreversible interventions. The progression culminates in ethical dissonance (compromised informed consent and non-maleficence) and terminal iatrogenic harm, creating a financial, physical, and psychological burden for the patient.


ABSTRACT

Background

Diagnostic errors in temporomandibular disorders (TMDs) contribute to unnecessary procedures and avoidable patient mismanagement despite advances in pain science, diagnostic classification systems, and evidence-based care.

Objective

To conduct a narrative review and present a dynamic, five-domain framework explaining how diagnostic uncertainty interacts with educational, cognitive, systemic, and ethical factors to produce iatrogenic overtreatment.

Methods

Searches of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar (inception to April 2026) identified literature on TMD diagnosis, clinical reasoning, dental education, health system organization, and bioethics. Concepts were synthesized into interacting thematic domains.

Results

Five dynamic, interacting domains were identified: (1) Educational Deficits, (2) Structural Reductionism, (3) Occlusal Overinterpretation, (4) System Fragmentation, and (5) Ethical Dissonance. The model demonstrates how educational gaps foster reductionist diagnostic paradigms, which are amplified by health-system silos and defensive clinical practices, increasing the likelihood of non-indicated, irreversible interventions.

Conclusions

The Five-Domain Framework offers a systemic model for understanding diagnostic breakdown in TMD management, providing a structured foundation for educational reform, integrated care pathways, and future empirical research.
